You are the AI assistant for Capitol Policy Review. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: Capitol Policy Review (CPR) is a nonpartisan, nonprofit newsroom based in Washington, DC, covering science and technology legislation in Congress. We publish explainers, vote trackers, and a weekly newsletter read by policy professionals. We do not take positions on legislation; our goal is accurate, fair, and useful coverage.

Current focus: One of our biggest stories this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup, can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
# S. 2817 (Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act): Drafting Review

This review covers the text as amended by the October 6 manager's amendment. I worked from the text alone and did not check it against the U.S. Code, the original bill, or the redline. The statutory references (DSHMRA, OCSLA, 28 U.S.C. § 2462, *Chadha*) should be verified before publication. The items below are questions a reporter would put to the sponsors and to committee staff, not positions.

**Definitions (§ 2)**

1. **§ 2(1)(B):** "The Secretary" is never identified. The bill does not say whether this is the Secretary of Commerce, Interior, or State, so it's unclear who makes the determinations and enforces the Act.
2. **§ 2(1)(B):** The Secretary can declare an activity to be commercial deep seabed mining, but the bill sets no procedure, notice, hearing, or deadline for that determination. Because § 5(b) makes willful violations a felony, a company could face criminal liability for an activity it had no prior notice was covered, which invites fair-notice and nondelegation challenges.
3. **§ 2(1)(B):** "Comparable" is undefined. It's unclear whether the comparison to subparagraph (A) is about tonnage, depth, or ecological risk.
4. **§ 2(1)(A):** The 10,000-ton threshold applies per "single vessel." Operators could split production across several vessels, each below the threshold, and the bill does not aggregate affiliated vessels or sites.
5. **§ 2(1)(A):** The bill doesn't say how tonnage is measured (wet or dry weight, raw nodules or contained metal, material recovered or processed) or how "per year" is counted. Without a measurement rule, the threshold is hard to verify.
6. **§ 2(1)(A):** "Recovery" is undefined, and "other mineral resources" is open-ended. It's unclear whether cobalt crusts, sulfide deposits, or sediment are covered.
7. **§ 2(1)(A):** The 200-meter depth floor means shallower seabed mining is outside the definition even at industrial scale. Staff should confirm this is intended and check for overlap with areas already regulated under OCSLA.
8. **§ 2(1):** The defined term "commercial deep seabed mining" has no profit or purpose element. Tonnage alone triggers it, so the word "commercial" is a label that could mislead readers.
9. **§ 2(2):** "U.S. person" covers only citizens and corporations organized under state law. It excludes LLCs, partnerships, trusts, and foreign-organized holding companies, which creates a structuring gap for the "anywhere" reach in § 3(a). "State" is also undefined: it's unclear whether D.C. and the territories are included.
10. **§ 2(3):** "Equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources" is undefined. It's unclear whether a vessel carrying stowed or detachable mining equipment qualifies.
11. **§ 2(3):** "Vessel" is undefined, so it's unclear whether barges, non-self-propelled platforms, or riser-lift systems count. The 5,000-GT threshold also covers only § 4; the prohibition in § 3 has no vessel-size limit, so the registry and the prohibition apply to different sets of operations.

**Prohibition (§ 3)**

12. **§ 3(a):** "Engage in" is undefined. The bill does not clearly reach financing, investment, equipment supply, processing, shipping, or contracting, so a U.S. person could arguably fund or service a foreign operation without violating the Act.
13. **§ 3(a):** "In the United States" is undefined, and the "anywhere" reach applies only to U.S. persons. Foreign-owned, foreign-flagged operations outside U.S. jurisdiction, including the Area and the high seas, appear to fall outside the prohibition. Staff should confirm this scope is intended.
14. **§ 3(a):** The bill has no savings or conflict clause for existing federal law. The Deep Seabed Hard Mineral Resources Act of 1980 already provides NOAA licensing and permitting for U.S. citizens, and OCSLA governs parts of the outer continental shelf. The bill does not say whether it repeals, amends, or runs alongside those regimes.
15. **§ 3(b):** "Exploration license" is undefined, and the bill doesn't name who issues it. The section heading refers to "existing operations," but the text covers licenses, not operations, so the heading and text don't match.
16. **§ 3(b):** The exemption has no limits on tonnage, duration, expiration, renewal, or transfer. A license could arguably allow commercial-scale recovery indefinitely, and nothing stops a license from being sold to a new operator.
17. **§ 3(b) and § 8:** The grandfather cutoff is the enactment date, but the prohibition takes effect 180 days later. Operators would have roughly six months of unrestricted activity, and the bill doesn't say whether conduct in that window is penalized.
18. **§ 3(c):** "Environmental assessment" is undefined, and the exemption has no limits on volume, duration, permits, or reporting. A commercial operation could recover large quantities and label them an assessment. The term also overlaps with NEPA's "environmental assessment," which could cause confusion.
19. **§ 3(c):** The bill doesn't say whether minerals recovered during an environmental assessment may be sold, retained, or processed.

**Registry and reporting (§ 4)**

20. **§ 4(a):** "Operator" is undefined. Vessels may have owners, charterers, and managers, and the bill doesn't say which one must register. No registration deadline is set.
21. **§ 4(a):** The bill does not specify what registration must include, such as beneficial ownership, vessel capacity, or operating location.
22. **§ 4(b):** "Recovery activities" is undefined, and the bill doesn't require any specific content in the quarterly report. Without tonnage, depth, and coordinates, the reports can't verify compliance with the 10,000-ton threshold or the § 3(c) exemption.
23. **§ 4(b):** No deadline is set for the first report, and the bill doesn't say whether a report is required when a vessel is idle.
24. **§ 4(b):** The reports rely entirely on operator certification. The bill gives NOAA no inspection, audit, data-access, or document-request authority.
25. **§ 4(b):** The bill doesn't say the reports are public. They could be withheld under FOIA Exemption 4 for confidential commercial information unless the Act requires disclosure.

**Penalties (§ 5)**

26. **§ 5 (general):** No enforcing authority is designated. The bill doesn't say who brings civil actions, whether administrative penalties are available, or what assessment, hearing, and appeal procedures apply.
27. **§ 5(a):** Penalties attach only to violations of § 3. Failure to register under § 4, late or missing reports, and inaccurate certifications carry no civil penalty as drafted. False statements would fall under general federal law, such as 18 U.S.C. § 1001, but the bill does not address them directly.
28. **§ 5(a):** The bill doesn't state a limitations period. The default five-year period in 28 U.S.C. § 2462 would apply, and it could outlast the Act's sunset.
29. **§ 5(a):** "Each day" is undefined, and the bill doesn't say whether penalties are counted per vessel or per operation. The bill also doesn't address inflation adjustment. The $1 million per-day cap may be a policy question for sponsors, not a drafting error, but it's worth asking.
30. **§ 5(a) and § 8:** Penalties apply to violations "occurring on or after the date of enactment," but § 3 takes effect 180 days after enactment. The two provisions are inconsistent.
31. **§ 5:** The bill has no injunctive relief, cease-and-desist authority, seizure or forfeiture of vessels or minerals, or in rem liability against vessels. It also has no citizen-suit or whistleblower provision. Each of these limits practical enforcement against foreign-flagged vessels.
32. **§ 5(b):** "Willfully" is undefined. The bill also doesn't address liability for corporate officers or for aiding and abetting, and it doesn't name the prosecuting authority.

**International agreement (§ 6)**

33. **§ 6:** "Shall seek to negotiate" imposes only an obligation to try. The bill doesn't require the Secretary to conclude an agreement, report to Congress, or face any consequence for failure. "Equivalent" is also undefined.
34. **§ 6:** The bill doesn't say whether an agreement would need Senate advice and consent or whether it would change domestic law. Its effect on the Act's own prohibitions is unaddressed.

**Duration and sunset (§ 7)**

35. **§ 7(a) and § 7(b):** Section 7(a) keeps the prohibition in effect "until" a joint resolution, but § 7(b) ends the entire Act after 10 years. The bill doesn't say which controls, so it's unclear whether the prohibition lapses at year 10 regardless of any NAS finding.
36. **§ 7(a):** "Serious harm" is undefined, and the bill sets no standard for the NAS report. It doesn't require Congress to commission the report, set a deadline, or fund it.
37. **§ 7(a):** The bill doesn't say whether the joint resolution must be presented to the President. Under Article I and *INS v. Chadha*, a resolution with legislative effect generally must be presented, which affects whether it can lift the prohibition. It's also unclear whether the finding alone ends the prohibition or whether the Act must be amended. No expedited procedure is provided.
38. **§ 7(b):** The sunset ends the entire Act. The bill has no savings clause for penalties on violations committed before the sunset or for enforcement actions still pending when it expires.
39. **§ 7(b) and § 8:** The 10-year sunset runs from enactment, so the Act is in effect for about 9.5 years. It's unclear whether that's intended.

**General**

40. **No severability clause:** If a court strikes § 2(1)(B) or the joint-resolution mechanism in § 7(a), the bill may fail as a whole. Sponsors may want a severability provision.
41. **Base text comparison:** This review covers only the amended text. Staff should compare it against the original S. 2817 to see which of these issues the October 6 amendment created or fixed.

**Top priorities before the October 15 markup**

- **Enforcement gaps (items 26–27, 31):** No enforcing agency is named, and the registry and reporting rules have no penalties.
- **Exemption scope (items 15–19):** The grandfather clause and the environmental-assessment exemption have no limits.
- **Discretionary definition (items 1–3, 36):** The Secretary's power to expand coverage, and the undefined "serious harm" standard, are the most likely targets for constitutional challenge.
- **Effective-date conflicts (items 17, 30, 39):** The bill's timing provisions don't align.
- **Sunset conflict (items 35, 38):** Section 7(a) and § 7(b) can't both be read as written.
